lesson_cards.title: Start with the right California electrical goal
lesson_cards.summary: A beginner should first distinguish four related goals: entering apprenticeship, qualifying as a certified electrician, preparing for C-10 trade licensure, and passing Law & Business.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner that these tracks overlap but are not identical. Apprenticeship is an earn-while-you-learn training path. General Electrician certification is a worker certification path under California DIR. C-10 is a contractor license classification requiring business readiness and trade competence. Law & Business is a separate contractor exam area.
teaching_points: Ask what role the learner wants: apprentice, employee electrician, contractor, or long-term owner.
Explain that a beginner can start with shared foundations before choosing a high-stakes exam path.
Separate eligibility facts from study content: eligibility is source-governed by Cognisphere; learning flow is Tutor-owned.
quick_check_prompts: Which goal is closest to becoming a licensed contractor: apprenticeship entrance, GE certification, C-10, or a basic math diagnostic?

lesson_cards.title: Career graph from applicant to contractor
lesson_cards.summary: The learner should see the electrical career as a staged graph: applicant, apprentice, worker certification, journey-level competence, contractor license, and business responsibility.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the graph as a set of routes, not one automatic ladder. An apprenticeship helps someone enter paid trade training. General Electrician certification is a California worker credential tied to qualifying work. A C-10 contractor path adds trade judgment, business law, qualifying experience, and license responsibilities.
teaching_points: Apprenticeship entrance is about selection readiness and documented eligibility.
Worker certification and contractor licensing are different legal roles.
Shared electrical foundations support every route.
A learner can study now while formal eligibility evidence accumulates over time.
quick_check_prompts: Which path most directly combines trade work with business responsibility: apprenticeship applicant, General Electrician worker certification, C-10 contractor, or paper-folding practice?

lesson_cards.title: Official source discipline
lesson_cards.summary: High-stakes exam and admissions facts should come from current official sources, not recalled questions or old internet summaries.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to separate stable learning concepts from update-sensitive facts. Topic weights, time limits, eligibility, allowed materials, application windows, and source editions must be verified against current official pages. Practice should use original questions shaped by blueprints, not leaked or recalled test items.
teaching_points: Official sources control exam structure and eligibility claims.
Blueprints guide study weighting without revealing live exam questions.
Recalled or leaked questions are unreliable and should not be used.
Tutor can teach from materialized claims while Cognisphere manages source freshness.
quick_check_prompts: For a real exam time limit, which source type is safest: current official page, copied forum memory, an old screenshot, or a random quiz bank?

lesson_cards.title: Diagnostic to readiness loop
lesson_cards.summary: The learning flow should repeatedly diagnose, teach, practice, tag errors, remediate, and then advance.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the loop as the learner's operating system. First diagnose the objective and weakest skill. Then give a mini-lesson, a worked example, a quick quiz, and targeted feedback. Every miss gets an error tag and a repair task. Advancement depends on evidence, not just finishing a page.
teaching_points: A diagnostic finds the next useful lesson.
Quick quizzes should be graded immediately.
Error memory prevents repeating the same miss.
Readiness gates decide whether to advance, review, or switch practice mode.
quick_check_prompts: After a wrong quick-quiz answer, what should Tutor do next: tag the error and remediate, ignore it, advance blindly, or ask for unrelated goals?

lesson_cards.title: Electrical math starts with units, ratios, and proportional thinking
lesson_cards.summary: Before code lookup or estimating, learners need reliable arithmetic, fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios, proportions, and unit conversion.
lesson_cards.body: Teach math as a field skill, not as abstract school review. The learner should translate word problems into quantities, units, relationships, and one operation at a time. Emphasize checking whether an answer is plausible before selecting a multiple-choice option.
teaching_points: Use units to decide whether to multiply, divide, or convert.
Use ratio tables for material quantities and scale problems.
Treat percentages as multipliers, especially for tax, markup, discount, and exam weights.
quick_check_prompts: A material costs $80 before 7.5% tax. Which expression represents the total: 80 + 0.075, 80 x 1.075, 80 / 0.075, or 80 x 0.075?

lesson_cards.title: Algebra and word-problem setup
lesson_cards.summary: Electrical calculations often fail because the learner solves before naming the unknown, units, and relationship.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a simple setup ritual: identify the unknown, list given quantities with units, write the relationship, solve one step at a time, and check plausibility. Use this for conduit length, voltage, current, resistance, loads, material takeoff, and business math.
teaching_points: Unknown first, equation second, arithmetic third.
Words such as per, total, remaining, increase, and twice signal operations.
Units reveal whether the answer is a length, rate, percent, current, or cost.
Substitution is useful when multiple-choice answers are numeric.
quick_check_prompts: If the problem says 'twice the shorter length plus 3 feet', what should be written before solving: 2x + 3, x/2 - 3, 3x only, or no equation?

lesson_cards.title: AC/DC and measurement basics
lesson_cards.summary: Before troubleshooting, learners need a plain-language model of AC, DC, meter choice, expected value, and safe verification.
lesson_cards.body: Teach measurement as evidence gathering. DC has one polarity direction; AC alternates. A meter reading only helps when the learner knows what should be present and where to measure. Safety comes before opening equipment or touching conductors.
teaching_points: AC and DC describe different voltage/current behavior.
A measurement point must match the question being asked.
Expected value matters before interpreting a meter reading.
Safe verification is part of the procedure, not an optional extra.
quick_check_prompts: Why is an expected value useful before using a meter: it lets you interpret the reading, it replaces safety, it removes units, or it proves every circuit is off?

lesson_cards.title: Drawings, tools, materials, and safety vocabulary
lesson_cards.summary: Beginners need vocabulary for plans, symbols, raceways, conductors, boxes, devices, tools, PPE, hazards, and jobsite instructions.
lesson_cards.body: Teach vocabulary as recognition in context. A plan tells what is intended, a symbol compresses information, materials become the installed system, and tools change how work is performed. Safety words should be learned early because instructions and warnings often decide the first correct action.
teaching_points: Symbols and drawings help locate devices, circuits, and equipment.
Tools and materials should be named by use, not memorized as isolated lists.
PPE, hazard, lockout, energized, de-energized, and verify are core safety words.
Reading jobsite instructions is part of trade readiness.
quick_check_prompts: Which word most directly means proving a condition rather than assuming it: verify, guess, rush, or decorate?

lesson_cards.title: Basic troubleshooting for beginners
lesson_cards.summary: Troubleshooting should move from symptom to safe verification to measurement to likely cause, not from panic to random replacement.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a beginner workflow: state the symptom, identify hazards, verify safe conditions, choose a measurement, compare expected and actual readings, isolate the likely cause, correct one thing, and verify the result. This same pattern supports GE, C-10, and jobsite learning.
teaching_points: Symptoms describe what is observed.
Measurements compare actual conditions with expected conditions.
Changing multiple things at once makes the cause harder to know.
Verification after correction prevents false confidence.
quick_check_prompts: A light circuit fails. What is the best first learning move: state the symptom and verify safe conditions, replace random parts, ignore measurements, or change every connection?

lesson_cards.title: Ohm's Law and power as the first electrical reasoning model
lesson_cards.summary: Voltage, current, resistance, and power form the learner's first reusable model for circuits, troubleshooting, and exam calculations.
lesson_cards.body: Teach V = I x R and P = V x I as relationships between cause, flow, opposition, and work. Keep the lesson practical: if resistance rises while voltage stays fixed, current falls; if current rises at the same voltage, power rises. Use this as a bridge to series, parallel, motors, overcurrent devices, and troubleshooting.
teaching_points: Voltage is electrical pressure, current is flow, resistance opposes flow.
Power connects electrical behavior to energy use and equipment load.
Most calculation errors come from wrong units or solving for the wrong variable.
quick_check_prompts: If voltage stays the same and resistance increases, what happens to current?

lesson_cards.title: Series, parallel, and combination circuits
lesson_cards.summary: Learners need to recognize how current paths change total resistance, voltage division, and power behavior.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the visual difference first: a series circuit has one path; a parallel circuit has multiple paths; a combination circuit mixes both. Then connect structure to calculation: series resistances add; parallel circuits create alternate current paths and need reciprocal or product-sum reasoning.
teaching_points: Circuit shape determines the calculation method.
Parallel branches do not behave like a single series chain.
Combination circuits should be simplified in stages.
quick_check_prompts: Which circuit type has only one current path: series, parallel, or combination?

lesson_cards.title: Inside Wireman aptitude test domains
lesson_cards.summary: The entrance test is not an electrical code exam; it checks math, numerical, reading, mechanical, and paper-folding reasoning under time pressure.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to treat aptitude preparation as five repeatable reasoning modes. Do not overteach NEC or contractor law here. The immediate goal is speed and accuracy on unfamiliar problems, plus disciplined reading of instructions.
teaching_points: Mathematical reasoning checks symbolic and word-problem setup.
Numerical reasoning checks patterns, data interpretation, and quantitative logic.
Reading comprehension checks careful extraction of meaning from technical text.
Mechanical and paper-folding tasks check physical and spatial reasoning.
quick_check_prompts: Which topic belongs to the Inside Wireman aptitude test: mechanics, contractor liens, NEC table lookup, or payroll taxes?

lesson_cards.title: Personal Experience Form as evidence, not an essay
lesson_cards.summary: PEF preparation should focus on accurate, supported evidence for relevant work, education, military, and life experience.
lesson_cards.body: Teach learners to organize PEF materials by claim and documentation. The form can materially affect ranking, so Tutor should coach completeness, accuracy, and evidence organization without inventing experience or overstating qualifications.
teaching_points: Each experience claim should have supporting documentation where available.
Accuracy matters because unsupported or inaccurate areas may not receive credit.
The learner should preserve original documents and submit within the required window.
quick_check_prompts: For PEF preparation, what is the safest strategy: exaggerate experience, submit unsupported claims, organize documented evidence, or skip the form?

lesson_cards.title: Apprenticeship entry: four-week test plan
lesson_cards.summary: For a near-term apprenticeship entrance selection, preparation should prioritize scoring reliability under time pressure.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a four-week plan around daily short reps: math setup, numerical patterns, technical reading, mechanical intuition, spatial folding, and mixed timed review. The learner should not try to learn the whole electrical trade before the entrance test. The goal is to recognize question type, choose a method, answer cleanly, and move on.
teaching_points: Spend the first days diagnosing which section is weakest.
Use short daily sessions instead of one long cram session.
Practice mixed sets because the real selection rewards switching modes.
Keep an error log with the reason for each miss.
quick_check_prompts: For a test next month, what should come first: deep NEC study, diagnosing aptitude section weaknesses, memorizing contractor law, or reading random exam dumps?

lesson_cards.title: Aptitude arithmetic speed
lesson_cards.summary: Entrance-test math needs fast, reliable arithmetic with fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios, and unit conversions.
lesson_cards.body: Teach arithmetic as recognition plus execution. The learner should identify the operation before calculating: combine, compare, scale, convert, or find a missing value. Emphasize scratch-work layout, estimating first, and rejecting impossible answer choices.
teaching_points: Fractions and decimals should be convertible without panic.
Percent questions often mean multiply by 1 plus or minus the percent.
Ratio questions become easier when total parts are counted first.
Unit labels prevent many wrong operations.
quick_check_prompts: A value increases by 20%. Which multiplier represents the new value: 0.20, 1.20, 2.00, or 20?

lesson_cards.title: Algebra setup for word problems
lesson_cards.summary: Most aptitude algebra errors happen before solving: the learner writes the wrong relationship.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to translate words into an equation in three passes: what is unknown, what relationship is given, and what units must match. Keep equations simple and original. The learner should solve after the setup is correct, not before.
teaching_points: Name the unknown before writing numbers.
Turn words such as total, difference, twice, per, and remaining into operations.
Check whether the answer fits the story.
If stuck, test answer choices by substitution.
quick_check_prompts: If x is doubled and then 5 is added to get 17, which equation matches: x + 2 + 5 = 17, 2x + 5 = 17, 5x + 2 = 17, or 17x = 2 + 5?

lesson_cards.title: Numerical reasoning and sequence patterns
lesson_cards.summary: Numerical reasoning rewards pattern testing: difference, multiplication, alternating pattern, grouping, and position-based rules.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a repeatable sequence checklist. First compare differences. If differences are not stable, compare ratios or multiplication. Then check alternating positions, paired groups, or a two-step rule. The learner should avoid staring at the numbers without testing a hypothesis.
teaching_points: Start with first differences.
If differences change, check second differences or multiply/add patterns.
Odd/even positions may follow separate rules.
A wrong answer often follows only the last visible jump.
quick_check_prompts: For 3, 6, 12, 24, __, which rule best fits: add 3, multiply by 2, subtract 3, or alternate plus 3 and plus 6?

lesson_cards.title: Data tables and graph reading
lesson_cards.summary: Numerical reasoning may require reading a small table, comparing rates, and choosing the right denominator.
lesson_cards.body: Teach table reading as a two-step process: identify what each row/column means, then decide whether the question asks for total, difference, rate, percentage, or trend. Many misses come from using the wrong row or comparing raw counts when rates are needed.
teaching_points: Read labels before reading numbers.
Ask whether the question wants a total, change, average, percentage, or ratio.
Use the same units before comparing values.
Circle the row and column being used in scratch work.
quick_check_prompts: A table question asks for percent change. What must you identify first: old value and new value, answer choice C, the longest row label, or the page number?

lesson_cards.title: Technical reading comprehension
lesson_cards.summary: Reading questions reward careful evidence, not outside knowledge or assumptions.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to answer from the passage. First read the question stem, then scan for the relevant sentence, then eliminate choices that add claims not supported by the text. In technical reading, small words like except, always, only, before, and after can decide the answer.
teaching_points: Use passage evidence rather than personal opinion.
Watch absolute words such as always, never, and only.
Sequence words such as before and after matter.
A correct answer may be plain rather than impressive.
quick_check_prompts: In a reading question, which is safest: answer from passage evidence, use outside trade knowledge first, pick the technical-sounding choice, or ignore qualifiers?

lesson_cards.title: Mechanical reasoning: levers and torque
lesson_cards.summary: Lever questions usually ask how force, distance from pivot, and balance relate.
lesson_cards.body: Teach levers with a simple rule: force farther from the pivot has more turning effect. The learner should identify the pivot, load, effort, and distances before choosing an answer. Avoid unnecessary formulas at first; build the physical intuition.
teaching_points: Find the pivot first.
A longer arm can reduce required force.
Balance depends on force times distance.
If both force and distance change, compare turning effect.
quick_check_prompts: On a lever, applying the same force farther from the pivot usually creates: more turning effect, less turning effect, no effect, or unrelated motion?

lesson_cards.title: Mechanical reasoning: gears, pulleys, and motion
lesson_cards.summary: Gear and pulley questions test direction, speed, force tradeoffs, and connected motion.
lesson_cards.body: Teach motion tracing. For gears, adjacent gears rotate opposite directions; linked belts or chains can preserve or reverse direction depending on configuration. For pulleys, more supporting rope segments can reduce required force but increase rope pulled. The learner should trace one connection at a time.
teaching_points: Adjacent meshed gears reverse direction.
Bigger and smaller gears trade speed and torque.
Pulley systems often trade force for distance.
Trace direction step by step instead of guessing from the picture.
quick_check_prompts: If two gears mesh directly and the first turns clockwise, the second usually turns: counterclockwise, clockwise, upward only, or not at all?

lesson_cards.title: Spatial reasoning: rotation and orientation
lesson_cards.summary: Spatial questions require tracking shape features through rotation without changing the shape itself.
lesson_cards.body: Teach learners to anchor one distinctive feature, then rotate the whole object mentally. Do not compare every line at once. Use corners, holes, arrows, shaded areas, or asymmetry as anchors. Eliminate choices that mirror instead of rotate.
teaching_points: Rotation preserves shape relationships.
Mirror images are common traps.
Anchor one unique feature before scanning choices.
Turn the page mentally, not the shape's internal geometry.
quick_check_prompts: In a rotation problem, what stays the same: relationships between features, the answer choice order, the printed orientation, or the time limit?

lesson_cards.title: Paper folding strategy
lesson_cards.summary: Paper folding questions test reflected positions, layers, holes/cuts, and unfold order.
lesson_cards.body: Teach folding as reverse simulation. Track the fold line, count layers, mark where a punch or cut passes through, then unfold one fold at a time in reverse. The learner should watch for symmetry and mirrored positions.
teaching_points: Unfold in reverse order.
A punch through folded layers creates multiple marks.
Each unfold reflects the mark across the fold line.
Symmetry is helpful, but only across actual fold lines.
quick_check_prompts: In paper folding, why can one punched hole become multiple holes after unfolding: because it passes through layers, because paper changes color, because holes move randomly, or because folds erase marks?

lesson_cards.title: Timed test strategy and skip rules
lesson_cards.summary: Aptitude performance depends on knowing when to solve, skip, mark, and return.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a practical pacing rule: easy points first, controlled attempts on medium questions, and fast skips for time traps. The learner should not let one puzzle consume the section. Review should focus on whether misses were knowledge, method, arithmetic, misread, spatial tracking, or pacing.
teaching_points: Do not spend unlimited time on one item.
Mark and return when a method is not visible.
Use elimination to improve odds when time is short.
Review errors by type, not by shame.
quick_check_prompts: If one spatial question is consuming too much time, what is usually better: mark and return, abandon the whole test, spend ten minutes on it, or ignore all easier questions?

lesson_cards.title: Test-day routine
lesson_cards.summary: The final week should protect sleep, documents, timing, and confidence rather than introduce many new topics.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a calm test-day routine: verify instructions, location, identification, allowed materials, arrival time, and any required portal steps from official communications. The final study day should use light mixed review and error-log refresh, not heavy new learning.
teaching_points: Official emails and portals control real logistics.
Sleep and arrival buffer are part of test readiness.
Use the final day for review, not brand-new concepts.
Bring only what official instructions allow.
quick_check_prompts: In the final 24 hours, what is most useful: verify official instructions and do light review, start a brand-new topic marathon, search leaked questions, or ignore documents?

lesson_cards.title: Application document checklist
lesson_cards.summary: The learner should separate test study from admissions paperwork so eligibility does not fail on missing documents.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a document-first routine: government photo ID, age requirement, diploma/GED/degree evidence, algebra proof, and later social security number at indenture. For transcripts and original documents, the learner should follow the local ETI instructions exactly because upload copies and boot-camp verification can differ.
teaching_points: A strong test score cannot fix missing required admissions documents.
Algebra proof is a gate for many electrical apprenticeship routes.
Original or official documents may be required later even when uploads start the process.
Veteran waiver documentation should be prepared only when the learner actually qualifies.
quick_check_prompts: Which is safest before studying all weekend: verify required documents and official instructions, assume documents can wait, upload unreadable screenshots, or invent missing experience?

lesson_cards.title: PEF 14-day workflow
lesson_cards.summary: The Personal Experience Form should be handled like a documented evidence packet with a hard deadline.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to list every relevant education, work, training, military, and community experience, then attach proof where possible. For LAETT, the PEF window and scoring impact make this a preparation task, not an afterthought. Tutor should help organize claims, not embellish them.
teaching_points: Write each claim only as strongly as the evidence supports.
Gather files before opening a timed or deadline-bound form.
Unsupported experience may receive no credit.
Track submission deadline, confirmation, and any official email instructions.
quick_check_prompts: If a PEF claim has no proof, what should the learner do first: document what can be verified, exaggerate details, submit unrelated photos, or ignore the deadline?

lesson_cards.title: GAN-style section map
lesson_cards.summary: GAN-linked sources describe aptitude preparation around math, reading, spatial reasoning, problem solving, and mechanical comprehension.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to map every practice question to a section before solving. LAETT names mathematical reasoning, numerical reasoning, reading comprehension, mechanical reasoning, and paper folding. GAN and California JATC comparator pages support a broader preparation map that also names numerical computation, problem solving, and mechanical comprehension.
teaching_points: Classifying the section tells the learner which method to use.
Math and numerical reasoning are related but not identical.
Paper folding is a spatial skill, not an electrical-code skill.
Electrical construction knowledge is not the center of aptitude preparation.
quick_check_prompts: A folding question belongs closest to which preparation bucket: spatial reasoning, payroll law, NEC lookup, or contractor bonding?

lesson_cards.title: No-calculator practice mode
lesson_cards.summary: Even when local instructions vary, no-calculator practice builds speed and reduces dependence on tools.
lesson_cards.body: Teach no-calculator practice as a conservative training mode, especially for arithmetic, percentages, ratios, and quick estimates. Comparator JATC pages explicitly prohibit calculators for some apprenticeship aptitude tests, so Tutor should prepare the learner to work cleanly on scratch paper unless the actual official instruction says otherwise.
teaching_points: Estimate before calculating to catch impossible answers.
Use fraction shortcuts such as half, quarter, fifth, and tenth.
Convert common percentages to decimals quickly.
Follow the actual test-day instructions for allowed materials.
quick_check_prompts: Why practice without a calculator: to build reliable mental setup, to avoid reading, to memorize NEC text, or to skip units?

lesson_cards.title: Reading elimination method
lesson_cards.summary: Reading-comprehension questions should be answered by evidence and elimination, one claim at a time.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a four-pass method: read the question, locate the evidence sentence, eliminate choices that contradict or add unsupported claims, then select the best remaining answer. Electrical Training Alliance sample guidance emphasizes that each sample question has one correct answer, which makes disciplined elimination valuable.
teaching_points: Do not reward choices that merely sound technical.
A wrong choice may be true in real life but unsupported by the passage.
Qualifier words often decide the answer.
One-correct-answer formats reward elimination under time pressure.
quick_check_prompts: If two reading choices sound plausible, what should decide: passage evidence, personal opinion, answer length, or the most technical word?

lesson_cards.title: Aptitude error log
lesson_cards.summary: The fastest improvement comes from naming the miss pattern, not simply counting wrong answers.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to tag each miss as concept, setup, arithmetic, misread, spatial tracking, mechanical trace, or pacing. The next study session should begin with the top two recurring tags. This keeps a four-week sprint focused and prevents random practice from feeling productive while leaving the same gap open.
teaching_points: Every wrong answer should produce a next action.
Method errors need a worked example; speed errors need timed repetition.
Misread errors need qualifier drills.
Spatial errors need slow reverse simulation before speed work.
quick_check_prompts: A learner misses three questions because they ignored 'except'. Which error tag fits best: misread qualifier, arithmetic, gear direction, or document upload?

lesson_cards.title: Application window and official messages
lesson_cards.summary: Admissions progress depends on completing online steps and responding to official scheduling instructions on time.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to treat online registration, document uploads, portal messages, and scheduling emails as part of the study plan. Different programs use different windows, so Tutor should teach the habit: read the current local instructions, make a deadline list, and verify status before test week.
teaching_points: Local official instructions override generic advice.
Online application completion and document upload are separate tasks.
Scheduling notices can arrive after staff review.
A calendar checklist reduces avoidable admissions mistakes.
quick_check_prompts: Which source should control a real deadline: the current official program page/email, a memory of a friend's process, a generic blog, or an old screenshot?

lesson_cards.title: Apprenticeship work expectations
lesson_cards.summary: The entrance process is for a real earn-while-you-learn trade path, not just a classroom exam.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner what the program is selecting for: ability to learn in class, work full time, follow safety instructions, read and understand English warnings, use tools, and handle physical construction conditions. This helps connect aptitude skills to job and school performance rather than treating the test as abstract puzzles.
teaching_points: Apprenticeship combines on-the-job training with classroom instruction.
Reading and safety-following matter because jobsite instructions can be high stakes.
Mechanical and spatial reasoning connect to tools, materials, and installation tasks.
A learner should prepare both for the test and for the reality of the trade.
quick_check_prompts: Why does an apprenticeship entrance test include reading and mechanical reasoning: because those skills connect to school/job performance, because it is a contractor license exam, because it replaces all training, or because NEC text is memorized?

lesson_cards.title: General Electrician eligibility baseline
lesson_cards.summary: General Electrician certification requires qualifying work experience and California-specific application rules.
lesson_cards.body: Teach eligibility separately from exam study. The learning plan can prepare knowledge, but eligibility evidence is a formal administrative requirement. The learner should understand the 8,000-hour baseline and the categories of work that may contribute to the total.
teaching_points: GE certification is tied to work under electrical contractors on NEC-covered systems.
Experience must come from more than one eligible work area.
Some categories have maximum credit caps, so not every hour counts the same way.
quick_check_prompts: Is GE eligibility only a matter of passing a knowledge quiz, or does it also require documented work experience?

lesson_cards.title: General Electrician exam blueprint and study weighting
lesson_cards.summary: GE study should be weighted toward Installation because the official outline assigns it the largest share.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to allocate time by exam weight: Safety is important but small in count, Electrical System Requirements is concept-heavy, Installation dominates the exam, and Maintenance/Repair is smaller but high-value for practical reasoning.
teaching_points: Use blueprint weights to avoid studying every topic with equal time.
Installation should drive the largest practice block.
Safety and maintenance still need spaced review because misses there are often preventable.
quick_check_prompts: Which GE domain should usually receive the most study time: Safety, Electrical System Requirements, Installation, or Maintenance and Repair?

lesson_cards.title: NEC navigation as a separate skill
lesson_cards.summary: Open-book GE preparation requires fast classification, article/table lookup, exception handling, calculation, and answer verification.
lesson_cards.body: Teach code navigation as a workflow. First identify the system or component in the question. Then classify the code topic, find the likely article/table, check definitions and exceptions, perform any calculation, and verify the selected option against the exact condition in the prompt.
teaching_points: Open-book does not mean slow-book: lookup speed is part of mastery.
Definitions, tables, and exceptions often decide close answer choices.
The learner should track lookup time separately from concept accuracy.
quick_check_prompts: In an open-book code question, what should happen before calculation: guess from memory, classify the code topic, ignore exceptions, or select the longest answer?

lesson_cards.title: GE installation domain: from wiring method to occupancy context
lesson_cards.summary: Installation practice should connect wiring methods, equipment, occupancies, lighting, HVAC, low-voltage, communications, and fire/life-safety systems.
lesson_cards.body: Teach installation as applied classification. The learner should learn to ask: What system is being installed? What wiring method or equipment is involved? What occupancy or environment changes the rule? Is this a communication, fire, lighting, HVAC, or power question?
teaching_points: Installation is the largest GE blueprint area.
Topic classification prevents wasting time in the wrong code article.
Special equipment and special occupancies change normal assumptions.
quick_check_prompts: A question mentions an installation in a special occupancy. Should the learner treat it like ordinary wiring only, or check the occupancy-specific requirements?

lesson_cards.title: GE sizing and calculation workflow
lesson_cards.summary: Sizing questions require the learner to identify the item being sized, the governing condition, the units, and the verification step.
lesson_cards.body: Teach sizing as a procedure, not a memorized answer. The learner should ask what is being sized: box, raceway, conductor, service, panelboard, clearance, termination, or overcurrent device. Then identify the condition, choose the route, calculate or compare, and verify the final answer against the prompt.
teaching_points: Sizing starts by naming the object being sized.
The same numbers can lead to different routes for boxes, raceways, conductors, or services.
Clearance and termination questions often hinge on condition words.
Final verification should compare units and exact prompt constraints.
quick_check_prompts: Before sizing a conductor, what should the learner identify first: the object and condition, the longest answer, a random table, or the previous question?

lesson_cards.title: GE maintenance and repair reasoning
lesson_cards.summary: Maintenance/repair questions reward safe diagnosis, test-equipment choice, component recognition, and verification.
lesson_cards.body: Teach maintenance and repair as scenario logic. A learner should identify the failed behavior, isolate hazards, choose the right measurement, compare expected and actual values, narrow the likely device or circuit issue, and verify after correction.
teaching_points: Maintenance questions are often smaller in blueprint weight but high leverage for practical skill.
Testing equipment is only useful when paired with a hypothesis.
Branch circuits, devices, and overcurrent protection should be diagnosed systematically.
Safe verification closes the repair loop.
quick_check_prompts: A breaker trips repeatedly. What is better first: diagnose conditions safely, replace every device, ignore the symptom, or assume the breaker is always bad?

lesson_cards.title: GE mastery dimensions
lesson_cards.summary: GE readiness should track concept knowledge, code navigation, calculation accuracy, timed accuracy, and lookup time separately.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner that one score is not enough. A learner may know the concept but look it up too slowly, calculate correctly but classify the topic incorrectly, or finish quickly while missing exceptions. Tutor should keep separate evidence streams so remediation is precise.
teaching_points: Concept mastery explains why an answer is plausible.
Navigation mastery finds the right source route efficiently.
Calculation mastery handles units and arithmetic.
Timed accuracy and lookup time show exam readiness under pressure.
quick_check_prompts: If a learner knows the concept but takes too long finding the rule, which dimension is weak: navigation speed, concept meaning, handwriting, or PEF documentation?

lesson_cards.title: GE sectional practice and full mock
lesson_cards.summary: Practice should move from single-domain drills to blueprint-weighted mixed sets and then a full mock only after route accuracy is stable.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a progression: first classify the domain, then do focused drills, then do small mixed sets, then sectional practice, and finally a full GE mock. After each session, score not only correct answers but also route choice, lookup time, calculation setup, and repeated error tags.
teaching_points: Blueprint-weighted practice prevents overstudying favorite topics.
Sectional practice isolates weak domains before a full mock.
Full mocks are useful only when reviewed deeply afterward.
Wrong answers should create remediation tasks.
quick_check_prompts: When should a learner move to a full GE mock: after some route accuracy and sectional stability, before learning any topic, after one lucky quiz, or instead of review?

lesson_cards.title: C-10 trade exam is closed-book contractor trade judgment
lesson_cards.summary: C-10 preparation should combine planning, rough wiring, finish work, startup/troubleshooting, maintenance, and safety.
lesson_cards.body: Teach C-10 as a contractor trade exam rather than a worker certification exam. The learner must reason from plans, costs, materials, sequence, installation quality, troubleshooting, and safety without relying on reference materials during the test.
teaching_points: Planning and Estimating and Rough Wiring are the two largest C-10 sections.
Closed-book testing rewards durable concepts and decision patterns.
Some questions require computation, so estimating math must be fluent.
quick_check_prompts: Is the C-10 trade exam open-book or closed-book according to the CSLB study guide?

lesson_cards.title: C-10 electrical calculation workflow
lesson_cards.summary: C-10 calculations should connect load, feeders, branch circuits, voltage drop, motors, transformers, grounding, and estimating decisions.
lesson_cards.body: Teach contractor calculations as decision support. The learner should identify the system, choose the quantity, set up units, compute cleanly, and decide what the answer means for material, labor, safety, or sequence. Closed-book practice should emphasize repeatable setups.
teaching_points: A calculation answer should support a contractor decision.
Load, feeder, branch, motor, transformer, and grounding questions need different setup routes.
Voltage drop and estimating calculations are common places for unit errors.
Closed-book readiness depends on pattern recognition and practice.
quick_check_prompts: In a C-10 calculation, why write units before arithmetic: to choose the right setup, to slow down for no reason, to avoid reading plans, or to replace safety?

lesson_cards.title: C-10 blueprint-weighted practice
lesson_cards.summary: C-10 practice should mirror CSLB section weights while staying original and closed-book.
lesson_cards.body: Teach practice planning from the blueprint: planning/estimating, rough wiring, finish wiring/trim, startup/troubleshooting/maintenance, and safety. The learner should see a mixed contractor scenario, classify the section, solve or decide, then review the error type.
teaching_points: Closed-book practice should build durable contractor judgment.
Planning and rough wiring should receive substantial practice time.
Safety cannot be treated as a tiny afterthought even if it is one section.
Mock review should separate content gaps from calculation and scenario-reading errors.
quick_check_prompts: Why use blueprint-weighted C-10 practice: to match official topic emphasis, to copy real exam questions, to avoid safety, or to skip estimating?

lesson_cards.title: C-10 estimating: scope, takeoff, material, labor, and risk
lesson_cards.summary: Planning and estimating questions test whether the learner can turn project information into quantities, costs, sequence, and code-aware decisions.
lesson_cards.body: Teach estimating as a disciplined chain: read plans and specifications, identify existing conditions, determine quantities, select materials, apply calculations, sequence the work, and account for project risks. Keep examples original and avoid copied exam items.
teaching_points: Quantity takeoff must match the drawings and specifications.
Material selection depends on application, environment, and code constraints.
Markup and margin are different business ideas and should not be confused.
quick_check_prompts: Which comes first in a takeoff problem: choosing an answer, reading the scope, applying sales tax, or ignoring drawings?

lesson_cards.title: C-10 safety: lockout/tagout, PPE, tools, hazardous materials, and site conditions
lesson_cards.summary: Safety is a distinct C-10 blueprint section and also cuts across installation, troubleshooting, and maintenance decisions.
lesson_cards.body: Teach safety as an action filter: before energizing, testing, replacing, or troubleshooting, ask what could harm people or property. Reinforce lockout/tagout, PPE, tool condition, hazardous materials, and jobsite environment recognition.
teaching_points: Safety questions often ask what should happen first.
The safest action may be procedural rather than technical.
Troubleshooting must not bypass de-energizing or verification habits.
quick_check_prompts: Before troubleshooting energized equipment, what kind of concern should be evaluated first: speed, color coding only, safety control, or brand preference?

lesson_cards.title: Law & Business blueprint
lesson_cards.summary: The Law & Business exam covers seven sections: organization/licensing, finances, employment, insurance/liens, contracts, public works, and safety.
lesson_cards.body: Teach Law & Business as scenario judgment. The learner should identify the role, obligation, document, deadline, money flow, employee issue, or public-works rule in the prompt before choosing an answer.
teaching_points: Contract Requirements and Execution and Employment Requirements carry the largest weights.
The exam is closed-book and multiple-choice with one best answer.
Business finance, insurance, liens, and safety should be learned through scenarios.
quick_check_prompts: Which Law & Business section is most directly about hiring, supervising, training, payroll, and records?

lesson_cards.title: Business organization and licensing cues
lesson_cards.summary: Law & Business learners should recognize entity, license, finance, payroll, tax, insurance, and employment cues before choosing an answer.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the learner to classify the scenario first. Is the question about business setup, license status, money, workers, insurance, tax, or records? The correct answer often depends on the legal or business role, not trade intuition.
teaching_points: Business organization and licensing are role-definition topics.
Finance, payroll, tax, and insurance are related but distinct obligations.
Employment scenarios often turn on worker status and required records.
Scenario classification should happen before answer selection.
quick_check_prompts: A question mentions hiring a worker and payroll records. Which topic family is most likely: employment requirements, paper folding, transformer sizing, or gear direction?

lesson_cards.title: Contractor qualifying experience
lesson_cards.summary: CSLB contractor exam eligibility is not just study readiness; applicants need qualifying experience in the classification.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the difference between being ready to learn and being eligible to apply. The learner can study early, but the formal contractor exam path requires qualifying experience and supporting documentation when requested.
teaching_points: CSLB states a four-year experience requirement for the classification.
Accepted roles include journey-level worker, foreman, supervising employee, contractor, or owner-builder.
Education or technical training may receive limited credit, but at least one year must be practical experience.
quick_check_prompts: Can a learner become exam-ready before being application-eligible?

lesson_cards.title: GE exam logistics and open-book discipline
lesson_cards.summary: Learners should understand exam logistics, scheduling authority, test-site materials, and why open-book still requires structured practice.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the exam process as part of readiness. The learner should separate three things: eligibility to apply, scheduling and candidate instructions, and content mastery. Open-book does not remove the need to know where topics live, because time pressure still punishes wandering through references.
teaching_points: Candidate instructions and scheduling processes can change, so Tutor should cite Cognisphere provenance rather than rely on memory.
Open-book preparation should include lookup route rehearsal, not only concept flashcards.
The learner should verify formal scheduling and allowed-material rules with the administering source before an actual exam date.
quick_check_prompts: Why is open-book GE practice still timed: because books are forbidden, because lookup route and decision speed matter, because all answers are memorized, or because no calculations appear?

lesson_cards.title: Symbols, plans, and diagrams
lesson_cards.summary: A learner must translate drawings and symbols into electrical systems before calculating or choosing code routes.
lesson_cards.body: Teach drawings as compressed jobsite instructions. Start by identifying the system, device, conductor path, panel or equipment boundary, then connect that picture to the question. The goal is not artistic drafting; it is reading enough of the diagram to know what work is being described.
teaching_points: Symbols reduce field objects to plan language.
A plan question usually asks for location, connection, sequence, material, or code classification.
Misreading a symbol can send the learner to the wrong formula or reference section.
quick_check_prompts: When a question includes a plan symbol, what should the learner identify first: the answer choice length, the represented device/system, the calculator key, or the exam timer?

lesson_cards.title: Conductors, cables, raceways, and wiring methods
lesson_cards.summary: Conductors and raceways connect electrical theory to installation decisions, sizing, protection, and code navigation.
lesson_cards.body: Teach wiring methods as a classification problem. The learner should ask what is being carried, where it is installed, what protection is needed, whether the environment changes the choice, and whether the question is about conductor, cable, raceway, box, termination, or support.
teaching_points: Conductor questions often combine ampacity, insulation, termination, protection, and environment.
Raceway questions often combine fill, support, bending, protection, and location.
The first decision is usually category classification, not arithmetic.
quick_check_prompts: A wiring-method question should first be classified by what: the system and installation condition, the longest answer, the learner's favorite formula, or the page number alone?

lesson_cards.title: Grounding and bonding as safety logic
lesson_cards.summary: Grounding and bonding should be taught as fault-current and touch-voltage control, not as isolated vocabulary.
lesson_cards.body: Teach grounding and bonding through the safety question: if something fails, where does current go, and how are metal parts kept at a safer potential? The learner should distinguish normal current paths from fault paths and connect that distinction to equipment, conductors, raceways, and overcurrent devices.
teaching_points: Grounding and bonding are safety and system-stability ideas before they are lookup topics.
Fault-current path reasoning helps explain why connections and continuity matter.
Many wrong answers confuse grounding, bonding, neutral conductors, and equipment grounding conductors.
quick_check_prompts: In grounding/bonding reasoning, what is the main safety concern: paint color, fault-current path, brand selection, or payroll records?

lesson_cards.title: Overcurrent protection and circuit protection
lesson_cards.summary: Circuit protection connects loads, conductors, faults, equipment ratings, and safety-first troubleshooting.
lesson_cards.body: Teach overcurrent devices as protection, not merely switches. The learner should understand that protection must coordinate with conductor capacity, equipment, fault conditions, and the system purpose. For exam practice, ask whether the question is about sizing, location, coordination, operation, or maintenance.
teaching_points: Overcurrent protection is a relationship between load, conductor, equipment, and fault behavior.
A tripping device is a clue, not a diagnosis by itself.
Troubleshooting should preserve safety controls before resetting or replacing parts.
quick_check_prompts: A breaker trips repeatedly. What is the safest learning response: keep resetting, identify the cause, replace with a larger device automatically, or ignore the load?

lesson_cards.title: Motors and transformers
lesson_cards.summary: Motors and transformers require learners to connect theory, sizing, protection, startup behavior, and troubleshooting.
lesson_cards.body: Teach motors as loads with startup behavior and protection needs, and transformers as devices that change voltage/current relationships while preserving power ideas within practical limits. Keep early lessons conceptual before moving into sizing and code navigation.
teaching_points: Motor questions often involve starting current, control, overload, and protection.
Transformer questions often involve primary/secondary relationships and equipment ratings.
Both topics reward a stable mental model before formula selection.
quick_check_prompts: Why should motor questions not be treated like simple resistive loads only: motors have startup/control/protection behavior, motors are never protected, motors ignore voltage, or motors are only paperwork?

lesson_cards.title: Testing and troubleshooting workflow
lesson_cards.summary: Troubleshooting should follow safety, symptom, measurement, hypothesis, correction, and verification.
lesson_cards.body: Teach troubleshooting as a workflow. Start with the symptom, confirm safe conditions, choose the right test instrument, measure one thing at a time, form a hypothesis, correct the likely cause, and verify the system works. This prevents random part-swapping and unsafe shortcuts.
teaching_points: The first troubleshooting step is often safety and verification, not replacement.
Measurements are useful only when the learner knows what value would be normal.
A good answer explains the next diagnostic step, not just a possible failed component.
quick_check_prompts: In troubleshooting, what should happen before replacing parts: verify symptoms and safe test conditions, guess from memory, skip measurements, or change multiple variables at once?

lesson_cards.title: C-10 rough wiring versus finish wiring
lesson_cards.summary: C-10 learners should distinguish hidden infrastructure work from visible final devices, trim, labeling, and startup checks.
lesson_cards.body: Teach rough wiring as the structural stage: raceways, boxes, panels, supports, conductors, and equipment placement before finish surfaces close. Teach finish wiring as devices, trim, labeling, terminations, testing, and handoff readiness. This distinction helps answer sequencing and constructability questions.
teaching_points: Rough wiring decisions can be costly to fix after walls or ceilings close.
Finish wiring focuses on final devices, trims, labels, connections, and verification.
Sequencing questions often ask what must be installed, inspected, or verified before the next trade step.
quick_check_prompts: Which task better fits finish wiring: setting concealed raceway before drywall, installing final devices and trim, excavating a trench, or calculating payroll tax?

lesson_cards.title: Special systems: PV, batteries, generators, and storage
lesson_cards.summary: Energy-production and storage systems require extra attention to system role, source behavior, isolation, labeling, and safety.
lesson_cards.body: Teach special systems by asking what energy source is present, whether power can flow when utility power is off, what isolation or transfer behavior matters, and what safety labels or procedures should be considered. Keep the lesson at concept and scenario level unless a verified code reference is present.
teaching_points: PV, generators, batteries, and storage change assumptions about where power comes from.
Isolation and labeling are central because multiple energy sources can be present.
C-10 preparation should connect special systems to planning, installation, startup, and safety.
quick_check_prompts: Why do battery or PV systems require extra safety attention: they may remain an energy source, they never need labels, they remove all code concerns, or they are only business paperwork?

lesson_cards.title: Contracts, bids, scope, and change orders
lesson_cards.summary: Law & Business learning should treat contracts and change orders as scope-control and risk-control tools.
lesson_cards.body: Teach contract scenarios around role, scope, price, timeline, changes, signatures, and documentation. A learner should not jump to a legal conclusion from one phrase; they should identify what document or obligation controls the situation and whether a change needs written approval.
teaching_points: Bids and contracts define expectations, scope, and money.
Change orders should be treated as documented scope changes, not casual conversation.
Many scenario traps confuse doing the work with documenting authorization.
quick_check_prompts: A customer asks for extra work outside the agreed scope. What should the contractor think about first: documented change authorization, ignoring cost, deleting the original scope, or skipping records?

lesson_cards.title: Employment, payroll, and worker records
lesson_cards.summary: Employment topics are one of the largest Law & Business areas and should be practiced as role-and-record scenarios.
lesson_cards.body: Teach employment requirements by distinguishing employee from subcontractor, hiring from supervision, payroll from tax, and safety training from general onboarding. The learner should learn to spot the worker relationship and the record or obligation attached to it.
teaching_points: Employment scenarios often ask who must keep a record or perform a required action.
Payroll, tax, insurance, and safety obligations are connected but not interchangeable.
Public works may add certified payroll and apprenticeship-related duties.
quick_check_prompts: Which clue points most directly to an employment-requirements question: worker hiring and payroll records, raceway fill, transformer voltage, or paper folding?

lesson_cards.title: Insurance, liens, and business finance
lesson_cards.summary: Learners need scenario-level distinctions among risk transfer, payment security, cash flow, markup, margin, and business records.
lesson_cards.body: Teach this cluster through contrasts. Insurance manages risk; liens relate to payment rights and notices; finance tracks money, cost, cash flow, taxes, markup, and margin. The learner should identify which business problem the scenario is really asking about.
teaching_points: Insurance is not the same as a lien or a tax record.
Markup and margin are different views of price and profit.
Payment-security scenarios require attention to timing, parties, and documents.
quick_check_prompts: A question asks how a contractor protects payment rights on a project. Which topic family is most likely: liens, circuit resistance, PV isolation, or paper folding?

lesson_cards.title: Public works, prevailing wage, apprenticeship, and certified payroll
lesson_cards.summary: Public works questions require learners to recognize government-project duties beyond ordinary private contracting.
lesson_cards.body: Teach public works as an extra compliance layer. The learner should spot when a project is public works, then consider contractor registration, prevailing wage, certified payroll, and apprenticeship-related duties. Keep advice general and tell learners to verify live requirements with DIR for real projects.
teaching_points: Public works status changes the compliance frame.
Prevailing wage, certified payroll, and apprenticeship requirements are separate but related duties.
A Law & Business scenario may hide a public-works clue in the project owner or funding context.
quick_check_prompts: Which clue most strongly suggests public-works compliance: government/public project context, a parallel circuit, a paper-folding pattern, or a residential light switch only?

lesson_cards.title: Law & Business scenario practice
lesson_cards.summary: Scenario practice should teach the learner to classify the issue, identify the responsible party, and choose the best compliant action.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a repeated scenario method: identify the parties, project type, document or duty, timing, and risk. Then choose the answer that best satisfies the obligation. Review wrong answers by whether the error was section classification, role confusion, timing, document evidence, or overgeneralization.
teaching_points: Start with who is acting and what role they have.
Look for documents: license, contract, change order, payroll, insurance, lien, or public works record.
Timing can change the correct answer.
Wrong-answer review should name the scenario cue that was missed.
quick_check_prompts: In a Law & Business scenario, what should be identified first: parties and duty, wire color only, paper folds, or a memorized slogan?

lesson_cards.title: Law & Business readiness
lesson_cards.summary: Readiness means the learner can make scenario judgments across sections, not merely recite isolated terms.
lesson_cards.body: Teach readiness as consistent performance across mixed scenarios. A learner should classify the section, explain why the chosen action fits, reject attractive wrong answers, and keep an error log. Mixed practice should include business organization, finance, employment, insurance, liens, contracts, public works, and safety.
teaching_points: Mixed scenarios reveal whether the learner can transfer knowledge.
One-best-answer questions require rejecting partially true choices.
Public works and employment scenarios often need extra attention to records.
Readiness gates should be based on evidence across sections.
quick_check_prompts: What best shows Law & Business readiness: correct mixed scenario reasoning, memorizing one definition, ignoring wrong answers, or only studying trade wiring?

lesson_cards.title: Cal/OSHA hazardous energy and lockout/tagout
lesson_cards.summary: Safety learning should include hazardous energy control as a procedural habit for electrical work and troubleshooting.
lesson_cards.body: Teach lockout/tagout as a safety workflow rather than a slogan. The learner should identify the energy source, isolate it, prevent unexpected energization, verify the condition, and restore only through a controlled process. Keep scenarios original and source-backed.
teaching_points: Hazardous energy control is relevant before maintenance, servicing, and troubleshooting work.
Verification matters because assuming de-energized is not the same as proving it.
Safety answers often prioritize controlled procedure over speed.
quick_check_prompts: What is the strongest reason for lockout/tagout practice: prevent unexpected energization, make paperwork longer, replace calculations, or avoid reading plans?

lesson_cards.title: Entrance Exam format: practice beyond multiple choice
lesson_cards.summary: Entrance Exam preparation should not assume every exercise is multiple choice; Tutor uses multiple formats to build speed, accuracy, and reasoning transfer.
lesson_cards.body: Teach that official selection materials describe tested abilities and sections, but local administrations may vary in exact item presentation. Tutor should train with multiple-choice checks for fast grading, numeric-fill items for arithmetic, short reading explanations for evidence discipline, and visual/spatial prompts for paper-folding and mechanical reasoning. Do not present original Tutor practice as leaked or official exam questions.
teaching_points: Multiple choice is useful for quick grading, but it is not the only readiness format.
Math and numerical reasoning need no-choice calculation practice.
Reading comprehension needs passage evidence, not outside assumptions.
Mechanical and spatial reasoning need step-by-step tracing before answer-choice selection.
Tutor practice is original and source-grounded; it must not claim to reproduce official questions.
quick_check_prompts: Why should an Entrance Exam learner practice numeric-fill and short evidence answers?

lesson_cards.title: Entrance math: fractions, decimals, and percent bridges
lesson_cards.summary: Fast aptitude math often depends on converting between fractions, decimals, and percentages without losing the base quantity.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the bridge method: fraction to decimal, decimal to percent, percent to multiplier. Always name the base before calculating. For selection practice, emphasize mental estimates first, exact arithmetic second, and answer plausibility last.
teaching_points: One half is 0.5 and 50%; one fourth is 0.25 and 25%; one eighth is 0.125 and 12.5%.
Percent increase uses increase divided by original amount, not the new total.
A decrease uses a multiplier below 1; an increase uses a multiplier above 1.
Estimate before computing so impossible answers are rejected quickly.
quick_check_prompts: A length increases from 80 to 100. What is the percent increase, and what base did you use?

lesson_cards.title: Entrance math: turn words into equations
lesson_cards.summary: Word-problem misses often come from translating the sentence incorrectly before any arithmetic begins.
lesson_cards.body: Use a four-step setup: define the unknown, mark total/change/rate words, write one relationship, then solve or test choices. Teach learners to slow down on words such as remaining, combined, per, twice, difference, and more than.
teaching_points: Define x in plain English before writing symbols.
Remaining means total minus used amount.
Per creates a rate: amount divided by unit.
Combined work or production often uses rates, not raw totals.
quick_check_prompts: Write an equation for: a worker has 12 more fittings than another worker, and together they have 64.

lesson_cards.title: Entrance numerical reasoning: pattern map
lesson_cards.summary: A repeatable pattern map helps the learner test common sequence and data patterns before guessing.
lesson_cards.body: Teach a short sequence checklist: constant difference, changing difference, multiplication/division, alternating two-track pattern, grouping, and position rule. For tables, compare rates and changes between rows instead of staring at isolated values.
teaching_points: First differences reveal many arithmetic sequences.
Alternating patterns split odd and even positions into two mini-sequences.
Table questions often hide the relevant denominator.
If two rules fit, prefer the simpler rule that explains every shown term.
quick_check_prompts: For 3, 6, 4, 8, 6, 12, what two-track rule is being used?

lesson_cards.title: Entrance reading: evidence ladder
lesson_cards.summary: Reading comprehension should be answered from passage evidence in a fixed order: locate, restate, compare, eliminate.
lesson_cards.body: Teach the evidence ladder. First locate the sentence that controls the answer. Second restate it in simpler words. Third compare each choice to that sentence. Fourth eliminate choices that add, reverse, overstate, or ignore a condition.
teaching_points: Do not answer from trade knowledge if the passage says something narrower.
Watch qualifiers: before, after, unless, except, only, first, required.
A choice can sound reasonable and still be unsupported.
For EXCEPT questions, mark the task before reading choices.
quick_check_prompts: What is the danger of choosing an answer because it sounds true but is not stated?

lesson_cards.title: Mechanical reasoning: force-distance tradeoff
lesson_cards.summary: Many mechanical items reduce to a tradeoff: less force usually means more distance, and more distance from a pivot increases turning effect.
lesson_cards.body: Teach learners to identify the moving part, the pivot or support, the direction of force, and the tradeoff. For levers, farther from the pivot generally needs less force. For ramps and pulleys, mechanical advantage usually exchanges force for distance or rope length.
teaching_points: Draw or imagine the pivot first.
Farther from a pivot gives more turning effect for the same force.
A longer ramp usually lowers required force but increases travel distance.
A pulley system can reduce pulling force while requiring more rope movement.
quick_check_prompts: Why does pushing farther from a hinge usually make a door easier to open?

lesson_cards.title: Mechanical reasoning: trace motion one connection at a time
lesson_cards.summary: Gear, belt, and pulley mistakes often happen when the learner jumps across the whole mechanism instead of tracing each connection.
lesson_cards.body: Teach one-connection tracing. Adjacent meshed gears reverse direction; gears connected by an open belt turn the same direction; a crossed belt reverses direction. Count reversals instead of relying on visual intuition alone.
teaching_points: Meshed gears reverse direction at each contact.
An even number of gear contacts ends in the same direction as the first gear.
An odd number of gear contacts ends in the opposite direction.
Open belts and crossed belts behave differently; inspect the connection.
quick_check_prompts: If gear A meshes with B, and B meshes with C, does C turn the same direction as A?

lesson_cards.title: Spatial reasoning: rotation is not reflection
lesson_cards.summary: A common spatial trap is treating a mirror image as a rotated object.
lesson_cards.body: Teach feature tracking. Pick an asymmetric feature, track its relative position, and ask whether clockwise order around the shape stayed the same. Rotation preserves the order of features; reflection reverses it.
teaching_points: Rotation changes orientation but preserves left-right handedness.
Reflection reverses the order of features.
Track one marked corner or notch before looking at answer choices.
If a feature swaps sides as in a mirror, it is not just rotated.
quick_check_prompts: What stays the same during rotation but changes during reflection?

lesson_cards.title: Paper folding: unfold in reverse order
lesson_cards.summary: Paper-folding problems become manageable when the learner reverses the folds one at a time.
lesson_cards.body: Teach reverse unfolding. Label the final folded packet, undo the last fold first, mirror holes or marks across that fold line, then undo the previous fold. Do not try to visualize the whole unfolded paper at once.
teaching_points: Unfold the last fold first.
Each unfolded layer mirrors marks across the fold line.
Count layers before deciding how many holes appear.
A mark on a fold line may duplicate differently from a mark away from the fold line.
quick_check_prompts: Why is reverse order safer than imagining the final unfolded page immediately?

lesson_cards.title: Entrance Exam daily cycle: lesson, drill, error memory, retest
lesson_cards.summary: Near-term preparation should alternate mini-lessons, short drills, named error memory, and retesting rather than long passive reading.
lesson_cards.body: Use a daily cycle: one mini-lesson, one worked example, three to six quick items, error label, then a retest later. The learner should know whether each miss was arithmetic, translation, evidence, mechanism tracing, spatial reversal, or pacing.
teaching_points: Short frequent practice beats one long theory block for aptitude readiness.
Every miss needs a label so remediation can target the cause.
Retest the same skill after a delay to confirm the fix held.
Final-week study should protect test-day execution instead of adding too many new topics.
quick_check_prompts: Name one error label that sends you back to math setup and one that sends you to pacing practice.

practice_blueprints.title: Apprenticeship aptitude mixed practice
practice_blueprints.summary: Generate original timed practice across math, numerical, reading, mechanical, and spatial reasoning.

practice_blueprints.title: Apprenticeship four-week sprint practice
practice_blueprints.summary: Generate original daily mixed practice for a learner preparing for apprenticeship entry selection early next month.
practice_modes: day 1 diagnostic across all aptitude sections
variation_policy: Rotate section focus daily while keeping one mixed review block.
Increase time pressure only after method accuracy is stable.
Generate original questions; do not use leaked, recalled, paid, or copyrighted exam-bank items.
Use explanations that identify error type: setup, arithmetic, pattern, misread, mechanical trace, spatial mirror, pacing, or documentation boundary.

practice_blueprints.title: Daily apprenticeship selection set
practice_blueprints.summary: Generate one short original set per study day: teach one method, ask one worked example, then grade three quick items.
generation_rules: Use only original Tutor-authored items.
Do not reproduce paid GAN study-guide content or official/sample items verbatim.
Use local LAETT requirements for admissions facts; use comparator sources only for practice shape.
After each quiz, tell the learner correct/incorrect, give the reason, tag the error, and either advance or remediate.

practice_blueprints.title: GE blueprint-weighted practice
practice_blueprints.summary: Generate original GE practice weighted toward Installation, with separate tracking for concept accuracy and NEC navigation speed.

practice_blueprints.title: C-10 closed-book scenario and calculation practice
